concepts.title: Inflation
concepts.askLine: What yearly rise in prices do you think India's central bank aims for?
concepts.hook: Five ₹20 idlis fit a ₹100 note; after each idli becomes ₹25, only four fit. The note has not changed. What did?
concepts.rule: Inflation is the yearly rise in prices across a basket of everyday goods. When prices rise faster than your money, it buys less. India's central bank aims for about 4%.

claims.text: India uses a consumer price index to track change in a basket of retail prices.
A rise in broad prices cuts the buying power of cash if its amount stays fixed.
India's inflation rate compares prices in one month with the same month a year earlier. Survey staff record prices in markets across India every month.
If income rises less than prices, real income falls; people on fixed incomes lose buying power.
India's inflation target is 4%, with a low limit of 2% and a top limit of 6%, set until March 2031. Falling prices can make people put off buying.

items.stem: Your hostel rent rises 8% this year, and your stipend also rises 8%. What happens to what the stipend covers?

options.text: It covers about the same as before.
options.feedback: Both grew at the same speed, so you are neither ahead nor behind on rent.

options.text: It covers more, because the stipend went up.
options.feedback: A raise only helps if it beats the price rise. Here they match, so nothing changes.

options.text: It covers less, because rent went up.
options.feedback: Rent rose, but the stipend rose just as fast, so the same share of rent is covered.

items.stem: Prices rise at the RBI's target rate for years. Your ₹20,000 savings account pays 3% a year. What happens to what it buys?

options.text: It buys a little less each year.
options.feedback: Yes. The target is about 4%, more than the 3% you earn, so prices outrun your savings.

options.text: It buys a little more each year, since interest keeps adding rupees.
options.feedback: The rupees grow, but only 3%. Prices rise about 4%, so each year the money covers less.

options.text: It buys the same, because the target keeps prices still.
options.feedback: The target is not zero. It aims for prices to rise about 4% a year, not to stay still.

items.stem: In a made-up example, the same basket costs ₹1,250 this May, 25% more than last May. About what did it cost last May?

options.text: About ₹1,000.
options.feedback: Yes. Last year times 1.25 gives ₹1,250, so divide 1,250 by 1.25 to get ₹1,000.

options.text: About ₹938, which is 25% off today’s price.
options.feedback: Taking 25% off the new price uses the wrong base. The 25% was added to last year’s price, so divide by 1.25.

options.text: About ₹1,563.
options.feedback: That adds another 25% on top. Going back a year means removing the rise, so divide by 1.25.

items.stem: Your pay rose 4% this year, yet it buys less than last year. What must be true about prices?

options.text: They rose by more than 4%.
options.feedback: Pay that buys less after a raise means prices grew faster than the raise did.

options.text: They rose by less than 4%, which made your raise shrink.
options.feedback: If prices rose less than your pay, your pay would buy more, not less.

options.text: They fell.
options.feedback: Falling prices would make the same pay buy more. Buying less points to prices rising faster.

items.stem: A friend says any inflation at all means the economy is in trouble. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Mild, steady rises are normal, since falling prices make people put off buying.
options.feedback: Right. A little inflation keeps people buying, which is why the RBI aims above zero.

options.text: He is right; the safest goal is zero inflation.
options.feedback: Zero is not the goal. Falling or flat prices can make people wait to buy, which slows things.

options.text: A falling price target would make people buy sooner.
options.feedback: Falling prices can make people put off buying. A little inflation is normal in the stated target.

items.stem: Put these in order to find how much your hostel mess bill rose in a year, in percent.

options.text: Find this month's bill and the bill for the same month last year.
options.feedback: You compare the same month a year apart, just as the inflation figure does.

options.text: Subtract to get the rise in rupees.
options.feedback: The gap between the two bills shows how many rupees more you pay now.

options.text: Divide the rise by last year's bill, then multiply by 100.
options.feedback: Dividing by the older bill turns the rupee rise into a yearly percent rise.

misconceptions.name: One price is the index
misconceptions.correction: One snack can rise while the broad basket moves in a different way.

misconceptions.name: Same cash, same goods
misconceptions.correction: When broad prices rise, the same cash can buy fewer goods.

misconceptions.name: Any raise makes you better off
misconceptions.correction: A raise smaller than the rise in prices still buys less than before.

misconceptions.name: The goal is zero inflation
misconceptions.correction: A little inflation is normal, since falling prices make people wait to buy. India's target is about 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.

steps.title: Inflation is prices rising across a basket

hook.stem: Say the news reports a 3% price rise (inflation) for May. What does that mean?

options.text: Everyday prices are about 3% above last May.
options.feedback: Right. It compares a big basket of everyday prices with the same month a year before.

options.text: Every single price rose by 3%.
options.feedback: Some prices jump and some barely move. The 3% is the overall change across the basket.

options.text: Prices rose 3% since April.
options.feedback: The figure compares this May with last May, a full year apart, not with the month before.

steps.teach: Inflation compares prices with the same month last year. India tracks a big basket of everyday goods, because one item, like onions, can jump while others stay flat.

example.ask: Tap the comparison.
parts: Rice, milk and bus fares in the big list
cost 3% more than they did last May,
so the news reports 3% inflation.
example.spot: cost 3% more than they did last May,
example.feedback: Inflation compares the same basket with the same month a year earlier.

guided.stem: Onions double in price, but most other prices barely move. What happens to inflation?
guided.hint: Onions are one item in a very big basket.

options.text: It goes up a little.
options.feedback: Yes. One item doubling moves the whole basket only a little when the rest stays flat. Each month is compared with the same month last year.

options.text: It doubles too.
options.feedback: Onions are a small part of the basket, so the overall rise is far smaller than double.

options.text: It stays the same, since one item does not count.
options.feedback: Onions are in the basket, so a big jump does move inflation, just a little.

steps.takeaway: Inflation is the yearly rise across a whole basket of prices.

steps.title: When prices outrun your money, it buys less

hook.stem: Your pocket money stays at ₹2,000 while prices rise 10%. What happens?

options.text: It buys about a tenth less.
options.feedback: Right. The note is the same, but each thing costs more, so the same money covers less.

options.text: It buys the same, since it is still ₹2,000.
options.feedback: The number on the money stays put, but prices moved up, so it now covers less shopping.

options.text: It buys 10% more.
options.feedback: Higher prices work the other way. The same ₹2,000 now covers less, not more.

steps.teach: When prices rise, each rupee buys less. So if your income grows slower than prices, you can buy less than last year, even with a raise.

example.ask: Tap why she is behind.
parts: Kavya got a 5% raise this year,
but her rent and groceries cost 7% more,
so her pay now buys less than before.
example.spot: but her rent and groceries cost 7% more,
example.feedback: Her costs grew faster than her pay, so the raise did not keep up.

guided.stem: A ₹100 basket of shopping now costs ₹125. How much of it does ₹100 buy?
guided.hint: Work out 100 divided by 125.

options.text: Four fifths of it.
options.feedback: Yes. 100 divided by 125 is 0.8, so the same cash covers 80% of the basket.

options.text: The whole basket.
options.feedback: The basket now costs ₹125, more than you hold, so ₹100 cannot cover all of it.

options.text: Three quarters, as prices rose by a quarter.
options.feedback: Close, but 100 divided by 125 is 0.8, so it buys four fifths, not three quarters.

steps.takeaway: If prices grow faster than your money, you fall behind.

steps.title: A little inflation is normal, and the RBI aims for about 4%

hook.stem: What inflation rate do you think India's central bank aims for?

options.text: About 4%.
options.feedback: Right. The RBI's target is 4%, with a band from 2% to 6% around it.

options.text: Zero.
options.feedback: The target is not zero. India aims for about 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.

options.text: 10% or more.
options.feedback: That would be far above the band. The upper limit is 6%, and the target is 4%.

steps.teach: A little inflation is normal, because if prices kept falling, people would wait to buy and business would slow. India aims for about 4%, in a 2% to 6% band.

example.ask: Tap why falling prices slow things.
parts: Prices drop a little every month,
so shoppers wait for an even lower price,
and shops sell less and hire fewer people.
example.spot: so shoppers wait for an even lower price,
example.feedback: When people expect lower prices later, they put off buying, and that slows the whole economy.

guided.stem: Inflation comes in at 7% this year. Where is that against the RBI's band?
guided.hint: Picture where the band starts and stops.

options.text: Above the 6% upper limit.
options.feedback: Right. 7% is higher than the 6% upper limit of the band.

options.text: Right on target.
options.feedback: The target is 4%. At 7%, inflation is above even the 6% upper limit.

options.text: Inside the band, near its top.
options.feedback: The band stops at 6%. At 7%, inflation is above the upper limit.

steps.takeaway: A little inflation is normal; India aims for about 4%.

concepts.title: Compounding
concepts.hook: ₹1 lakh growing at an example rate of 7% for 30 years becomes about ₹7.6 lakh. The last ten years add more than the first twenty.
concepts.rule: Compounding means a gain can earn a later gain when it stays in the pot. A SIP adds money at set times, but that does not promise a set return.

claims.text: Compound growth includes growth on past gains as well as the starting amount.
A SIP is a way to add money at set times; market returns are not fixed, because investments can rise or fall in value.
Saved at 5% a year, 365 grows to about 466 after five years and about 1,578 after thirty years.
The sooner saving starts, the more time compound interest has to build it up.

items.stem: A club's page has 2,000 followers and grows 10% a month. Each month's gain is worked on the new total, like compound interest. About how many followers after two months?

options.text: About 2,420.
options.feedback: Month one adds a tenth to make 2,200. Month two adds a tenth of 2,200, so the page ends near 2,420.

options.text: About 2,400.
options.feedback: That adds the same gain twice. Month two works on the bigger total, so it adds more than month one.

options.text: About 4,000.
options.feedback: That doubles the page. Two months at 10% add only about a fifth, so it ends near 2,420.

items.stem: Tanvi says ₹3,000 at 10% a year for three years adds exactly ₹900 if gains stay in. What is she missing?

options.text: Each year, 10% works on a bigger sum.
options.feedback: Kept gains grow the base, so the years add ₹300, ₹330 and ₹363. That is ₹993, not ₹900.

options.text: The 10% counts in the first year, then stops.
options.feedback: The rate applies every year. Each year it works on the sum plus the gains kept in.

options.text: She is right; three years of 10% is ₹900.
options.feedback: That treats each year as earning on the first ₹3,000 only. Kept gains earn too, so it adds ₹993.

items.stem: Nafisa puts ₹10,000 away at 21. Bikash starts at 26 at the same rate and wants as much as Nafisa at 50. What must Bikash do?

options.text: Put in more than ₹10,000.
options.feedback: Yes. His money has five fewer years to grow, so he needs a bigger start to catch up.

options.text: Put in the same ₹10,000.
options.feedback: The same sum with fewer years ends smaller, because it has less time to build on gains.

options.text: Put in less, since he starts later and saves on time.
options.feedback: Starting later gives less time to grow, not more. He needs a bigger sum, not a smaller one.

items.stem: Dinesh keeps ₹8,000 in a locker at home for 25 years, where it earns nothing. What does all that time add to it?

options.text: Nothing, as there is no gain to build on.
options.feedback: Right. Compounding needs a gain to grow on. At 0% the ₹8,000 stays ₹8,000, and rising prices make it buy less.

options.text: A lot, since long spans do most of the work.
options.feedback: Time only helps when the money earns something. With no gain each year, there is nothing to compound.

options.text: It doubles, as 25 years is a long wait.
options.feedback: Doubling needs a yearly gain. Money that earns 0% stays the same size, however long it waits.

items.stem: A SIP can still lose money in a bad year, because ___.

options.text: the fund's investments can fall in price
options.feedback: Yes. A SIP sets the sum and the dates, but what the fund holds can still drop in value.

options.text: a fixed SIP return turns negative in a bad year
options.feedback: A SIP sets when money is added, not its return. The fund can lose value when its investments fall.

options.text: a SIP pays a fixed rate like a bank deposit
options.feedback: A SIP has no fixed rate. Its value moves with what the fund holds, so it can fall.

items.stem: Two friends run ₹2,000 monthly SIPs in the same fund. One starts at 22, one at 30, and both stop at 50. What can you say?

options.text: The early starter will likely end with more, but neither result is promised.
options.feedback: Right. More years give more time to compound, yet the market still sets the actual growth.

options.text: Both end the same, since they pay the same each month.
options.feedback: The early starter pays for more years, and those years also have longer to grow.

options.text: The early starter is sure to end with twice as much.
options.feedback: No SIP result is sure. The market sets the growth, so no exact amount can be promised.

misconceptions.name: Gain only on start
misconceptions.correction: When gains stay in the pot, later gains can build on them too.

misconceptions.name: SIP means sure gain
misconceptions.correction: A SIP sets a payment pattern; it does not set market returns.

misconceptions.name: A late start costs nothing
misconceptions.correction: Starting later gives money fewer years to grow, so it ends smaller.

misconceptions.name: Interest only grows the first amount
misconceptions.correction: Compound growth includes gains on past gains as well as on the starting amount.

misconceptions.name: Time alone compounds idle cash
misconceptions.correction: Compound growth needs gains; cash that earns nothing has no gains to build on.

steps.title: Gains start earning gains

hook.stem: Gurleen and Om each save ₹1,000 at 10%. Gurleen leaves her interest in; Om spends his. Who has more after two years?

options.text: Gurleen, with ₹1,210.
options.feedback: Right. Her ₹100 gain stayed in and earned ₹10 more in year two.

options.text: Both have ₹1,200.
options.feedback: Om has ₹1,000 plus ₹200 spent. Gurleen's kept gain earned extra, so she has ₹1,210.

options.text: Om, since he took ₹200 out.
options.feedback: Spending the interest means it cannot earn more. Gurleen ends with ₹1,210 saved.

steps.teach: With compound interest, you earn on your savings and on the interest they already made. So each year's gain is a bit bigger.

example.ask: Tap the balance on which year two's interest is worked out.
parts: Lakshmi saved ₹1,000, and it earned ₹100 in year one.
Year two's interest was worked out on ₹1,100,
so her balance grew to ₹1,210.
example.spot: Year two's interest was worked out on ₹1,100,
example.feedback: Year two's 10% worked on ₹1,100: her first ₹1,000 plus the ₹100 gain she left in.

guided.stem: ₹500 grew to ₹550 in year one, with the gain left in. In year two it earns 10% again. How big is the new gain?
guided.hint: Work out the rate on the new total, not on the first sum.

options.feedback: Right. The rate now works on ₹550, so the gain grows to ₹55.
That is 10% of the old ₹500. The pot is now ₹550, so the gain is ₹55.
That is only the gain on last year's gain. The full gain is 10% of ₹550, or ₹55.

steps.takeaway: Gains you leave in start to earn gains too.

steps.title: Time does most of the work

hook.stem: You save ₹365 once at 5% a year and leave it. About how much is it after 30 years?

options.text: About ₹1,578.
options.feedback: Right. Growth on growth for 30 years takes ₹365 to about ₹1,578.

options.text: About ₹913.
options.feedback: That counts 5% of ₹365 each year, as if gains never earned. Compounding gives about ₹1,578.

options.text: About ₹466.
options.feedback: That is the value after five years. Twenty-five more years take it near ₹1,578.

steps.teach: Growth on growth starts slow and speeds up, because each year’s gain is worked on a bigger pot. Saved at 5%, ₹365 becomes about ₹1,578 in thirty years.

example.ask: Tap why Gurpreet ends with more.
parts: Gurpreet and Prakash both save at the same rate,
but Gurpreet starts ten years sooner,
so her money has longer to grow.
example.spot: but Gurpreet starts ten years sooner,
example.feedback: The same rate gives more when it has more years to work on past gains.

guided.stem: Over 30 years at 5%, which five years add the most rupees?
guided.hint: Ask when the pot is at its biggest.

options.text: The last five years.
options.feedback: Right. By then the pot is largest, so the same 5% adds the most rupees.

options.text: The first five years.
options.feedback: The pot is smallest then, so 5% adds the fewest rupees.

options.text: Every five-year span adds the same.
options.feedback: Each span starts from a bigger pot, so later spans add more.

steps.takeaway: The longer money grows, the faster it grows.

steps.title: A SIP is a habit, not a promise

hook.stem: A SIP takes ₹500 from your account every month. What does it fix?

options.text: How much goes in, and when.
options.feedback: Right. A SIP sets the sum and the dates. The market sets the return.

options.text: The return you will earn.
options.feedback: A SIP does not fix the return. The fund's value moves with the market.

options.text: That the fund keeps going up.
options.feedback: Funds can fall as well as rise. A SIP just keeps adding money on set dates.

steps.teach: A SIP (systematic investment plan) puts in the same sum at set times, like ₹500 each month. It cannot set the growth, because the fund’s investments rise and fall.

example.ask: Tap the part a SIP cannot promise.
parts: Anil sets up a ₹1,000 SIP each month,
the money goes in on the 5th,
and the fund's value moves with the market.
example.spot: and the fund's value moves with the market.
example.feedback: Anil controls the sum and the date. The market decides how the fund's value moves.

guided.stem: Your SIP buys fewer fund units this month than last month, though you paid the same ₹500. Which part stayed fixed?
guided.hint: Ask what you chose when you set it up.

options.text: The ₹500 and the date.
options.feedback: Right. You set the sum and the date. The unit price rose, so the same ₹500 bought fewer units.

options.text: The price of each fund unit.
options.feedback: The unit price moved. A higher price is why the same ₹500 bought fewer units this month.

options.text: The 12% a year that SIPs give.
options.feedback: No SIP fixes a return. Only the sum and the date stay set; the fund's price moves.

steps.takeaway: A SIP fixes what you put in, not what you get back.

concepts.title: The rule of 72
concepts.hook: At an example rate of 9%, 72 ÷ 9 says eight years to double. Working it out exactly gives close to eight, but not exactly eight.
concepts.rule: For a steady percent rate, divide 72 by the rate to guess the years to double. It works for unpaid debt too. It is a rough shortcut, not a promise of market growth.

claims.text: The rule of 72 is a rough way to guess when a sum may double. Divide 72 by a set rate.
Market returns do not have a fixed rate, so the shortcut is only a what-if tool there.
At 4% a year, savings double in about 18 years, since 72 divided by 4 is 18.
The rule works for debt too: an unpaid card balance at 18% interest doubles in about four years. One large Indian card issuer charges up to 3.75% a month, or 45% a year.

items.stem: Prices rise at a steady 3% a year. By the shortcut, about how many years until prices double?

options.text: About 24 years.
options.feedback: The shortcut works for any steady rate, prices too. 72 divided by 3 gives about 24 years.

options.text: About 3 years.
options.feedback: The rate is not the time. Dividing 72 by 3 gives about 24 years for prices to double.

options.text: About 216 years.
options.feedback: That multiplies 72 by 3. The rule divides 72 by the rate, which gives about 24.

items.stem: Your ₹50,000 deposit pays a steady 7%. The shortcut gives about 10.3 years to double. What should you expect?

options.text: About ten years; the shortcut is close, not exact.
options.feedback: Right. Worked out exactly it is about 10.2 years, near the guess but not the same.

options.text: Exactly 10.3 years, to the day.
options.feedback: The rule is a quick guess. The real time is close to it but not an exact date.

options.text: Far longer, since the shortcut is usually way off.
options.feedback: For steady rates like this the guess is close. Here the exact answer is about 10.2 years.

items.stem: You owe ₹8,000 on a card. Each month you pay all the interest, but none of the ₹8,000. What happens to the balance?

options.text: It stays at ₹8,000.
options.feedback: Yes. No interest is left unpaid, so nothing is added and the debt cannot double.

options.text: It still doubles on the usual timeline.
options.feedback: Debt doubles only when unpaid interest is added on. Here all of it is paid each month.

options.text: It falls a little every month.
options.feedback: Paying only interest keeps the debt level. To shrink it, part of the ₹8,000 must be paid too.

items.stem: You have ₹15,000 saved at 8% and owe ₹15,000 on a card at 45%. Which doubles first, and about when?

options.text: The debt, in under two years.
options.feedback: Right. 72 ÷ 45 is about 1.6, while the savings need 72 ÷ 8, about nine years.

options.text: The savings, in about nine years.
options.feedback: Nine years is right for the savings, but the debt doubles far sooner, in under two years.

options.text: Both in about the same time, since they start equal.
options.feedback: Starting sums match, but rates do not. A higher rate doubles much faster.

items.stem: A fund doubled in about 8 years, though its return went up and down each year. Using the doubling shortcut backwards, about what steady rate would have done the same?

options.text: About 9% a year.
options.feedback: Right. 72 divided by 8 gives about 9%. It is the steady rate that matches, not what the fund earned each year.

options.text: Exactly 9% in each of the eight years.
options.feedback: Its return went up and down, so no single year had to be 9%. The 9% is only a steady stand-in.

options.text: About 64%.
options.feedback: That multiplies 8 by 8. Going backwards, the shortcut divides 72 by the years, giving about 9%.

items.stem: The doubling shortcut gives a fair answer only when ___.

options.text: the rate stays the same each year
options.feedback: Right. Dividing 72 by a rate assumes that rate holds every year, as with a fixed deposit.

options.text: the sum is bigger than ₹1 lakh at the start
options.feedback: The size of the sum does not matter. What matters is whether the rate holds still year after year.

options.text: the money sits in shares
options.feedback: Share returns jump around from year to year, so for them the shortcut is only a what-if.

misconceptions.name: Exact clock
misconceptions.correction: The rule gives a rough guess, not an exact date.

misconceptions.name: Any market rate is fixed
misconceptions.correction: Market gains can vary; the shortcut needs a steady assumed rate.

misconceptions.name: Debt stays the same size
misconceptions.correction: Unpaid debt gathers interest too, and a high rate doubles it fast.

hook.stem: Money grows at a steady 6% a year. About how long until it doubles?

options.text: About 12 years.

options.text: About 6 years.
options.feedback: That uses the rate as the years. Divide 72 by 6 to get about 12.

so they double in about 18 years.

example.feedback: Dividing 72 by the rate gives the rough number of years to double.

guided.stem: At 8% a year, money doubles in about 9 years. About what is ₹5,000 worth after 18 years?
guided.hint: Count how many 9-year spans fit in 18 years.

options.feedback: Right. In 18 years it doubles twice: ₹5,000 to ₹10,000, then ₹10,000 to ₹20,000.

options.text: About ₹10,000, as it doubles once.
options.feedback: That is one doubling, which takes 9 years. The next 9 years double it again, to ₹20,000.
That adds the same ₹5,000 gain twice. The second doubling works on ₹10,000, so it ends near ₹20,000.

steps.takeaway: Years to double is about 72 divided by the rate.

steps.title: Debt doubles the same way

hook.stem: A card balance of ₹10,000 is left unpaid at 36% a year. About when does it reach ₹20,000?

options.text: In about 2 years.
options.feedback: Right. 72 ÷ 36 is 2, so unpaid card debt at that rate doubles in about two years.

options.text: In about 36 years.
options.feedback: The rate is not the years. 72 divided by 36 gives about two.

options.text: Never, with no new spending.
options.feedback: Interest keeps adding to the unpaid balance, so it grows on its own.

steps.teach: The rule works on debt too, because unpaid interest is added to what you owe and earns interest. At 36% a year, card debt doubles in about two years.

example.ask: Tap why the debt doubles.
parts: Arav owes ₹5,000 on a card at 36% a year,
and he leaves it unpaid,
so in about two years he owes near ₹10,000.
example.spot: and he leaves it unpaid,
example.feedback: An unpaid balance keeps gathering interest, so 36% doubles it in about two years.

guided.stem: Which grows faster: savings at 6% or a debt at 18%?
guided.hint: Work out the doubling time for each one.

options.text: The 18% debt.
options.feedback: Right. It doubles in about 4 years; the savings take about 12. Some Indian cards charge up to 45% a year, which is faster still.

options.text: The savings; an unpaid debt does not grow by itself.
options.feedback: Unpaid interest is added to the debt and earns interest too, so at 18% it doubles in about 4 years.

options.text: The savings; debt stays put.
options.feedback: Unpaid interest is added to a debt, so it grows like savings do, only faster here.

steps.takeaway: High-interest debt doubles fast; at 36% it takes about two years.

steps.title: Only for a steady rate

hook.stem: A fund gained 20% last year and fell 5% this year. What does 72 ÷ 20 tell you about it?

options.text: Not much, as the rate did not stay steady.
options.feedback: Right. The rule needs one rate that holds. This fund's return jumped around.

options.text: It will double in 3.6 years.
options.feedback: That would need 20% every year. Last year's gain is no promise.

options.text: It will double in 72 years.
options.feedback: 72 is only the number you divide. The real issue is that the rate changes.

steps.teach: For shares, the rule can only say: if it grew 12% every year, it would double in 6. Real years go up and down, so no single rate fits.

example.ask: Tap the part that breaks the shortcut.

then dropped 10% the next,
so 72 ÷ 15 cannot give its doubling time.
example.spot: then dropped 10% the next,
example.feedback: The return changed from year to year, so no single rate fits the rule.

guided.stem: Which case suits the rule of 72 best?
guided.hint: Look for a number that holds still.

options.text: A deposit at a fixed 6%.
options.feedback: Yes. A fixed rate is just what the rule needs.

options.text: A share that rose 30% last year.
options.feedback: One good year does not set future returns, so the rule is only a what-if here.

options.text: An index fund that averaged 12% for ten years.
options.feedback: An average hides up and down years, so the rule is only a what-if here.

steps.takeaway: The rule needs a steady rate; markets do not give one.

concepts.title: Risk and return
concepts.hook: A sure ₹12, or a coin flip for ₹30 or nothing. The flip could pay more, or nothing. The range of results matters.
concepts.rule: A bigger possible gain often comes with more chance of loss or a wider range of results. A high possible return is not a sure return.

claims.text: Investment risk includes the chance of loss and uncertain results.
A high possible gain may mean more risk. The gain is not sure.

Cash savings are the safest of the three main kinds of assets but earn the least; shares carry the most risk and have earned the most over time. A bond is a loan to a company, and investors want higher returns for taking more risk.
In the US, large company shares as a group have dropped in value in about one year out of every three.
A longer time to a goal gives more room to wait out ups and downs; money needed soon usually suits lower-risk places.

items.stem: Your shares came back at ₹2,700, a 10% loss on what you put in. About what did you put in?

options.text: About ₹3,000.
options.feedback: Yes. A 10% loss leaves nine tenths, and nine tenths of ₹3,000 is ₹2,700.

options.text: About ₹2,970, adding 10% of ₹2,700 back.
options.feedback: The 10% was taken from the start, not from ₹2,700. Divide ₹2,700 by 0.9 to get ₹3,000.

options.text: About ₹2,430.
options.feedback: That takes another 10% off. Going back to the start means undoing the loss, which gives ₹3,000.

items.stem: Money you need in a few months fits low-risk savings, because ___.

options.text: a drop could hit just when you need it
options.feedback: Right. Short-term money has no time to wait for a fall to recover, so a low-risk place fits it.

options.text: savings earn more than shares over time
options.feedback: Over long spans, shares have usually earned more. Savings fit here because they swing less, not because they earn more.

options.text: shares cannot move much in a few months
options.feedback: Share prices can move a lot in a few months. That is why money needed soon suits low-risk savings.

items.stem: Two summer jobs: one pays a sure ₹6,000. The other pays sales commission, anywhere from ₹0 to ₹15,000. Which one carries risk?

options.text: The commission job.
options.feedback: Yes. Its result is unsure and could be zero. That chance of getting less than hoped is risk.

options.text: The fixed-pay job, since it cannot pay more.
options.feedback: Missing out on a bigger amount is not the risk here. The fixed job's result is known in advance.

options.text: Neither, since both are honest work.
options.feedback: Risk is not about honesty. It is about how unsure the result is, and only one pay is unsure.

items.stem: A college friend's crypto app is up 40% this month. What does that tell you about next month?

options.text: Nothing sure; big jumps can reverse just as fast.
options.feedback: Right. Things that rise sharply also swing sharply, so a big gain is no promise of the next one.

options.text: It will rise about 40% again.
options.feedback: One month sets no pattern. Bigger possible gains come with bigger possible falls.

options.text: It has become a low-risk choice.
options.feedback: A sharp rise shows big swings, which is the mark of more risk, not less.

items.stem: Cash is the safest of the three main kinds. What risk does it still carry?

options.text: Rising prices can shrink what it buys.
options.feedback: Yes. Cash rarely loses rupees, but if prices rise faster than it earns, it buys less.

options.text: None, since its rupee value holds still.
options.feedback: The rupee amount holds, but rising prices can still cut what it buys over time.

options.text: Cash savings swing like shares but earn more over time.
options.feedback: Cash savings have been steadier and earned less than shares. Rising prices can still cut what cash buys.

items.stem: You need ₹20,000 in 6 months, and ₹2 lakh in 28 years. Where does each fit?

options.text: Savings for the first; more swing suits the second.
options.feedback: Yes. Money needed soon has no time to recover, while a far goal can ride out dips.

options.text: Shares for both, to earn the most.
options.feedback: Shares could drop just before the 6-month goal, with no time to recover.

options.text: Savings for both, since cash has earned more than shares.
options.feedback: Cash savings have earned less than shares over time. The distant goal has more room to wait out swings.

misconceptions.correction: An uncertain asset can lose value as well as gain it.

misconceptions.correction: Shares of large, famous firms can drop in value too.

misconceptions.correction: Cash savings have earned less than shares over time, though shares carry more risk.

misconceptions.correction: Share values can fall, so money needed soon usually suits a lower-risk place.

concepts.title: Diversification
concepts.hook: A monsoon cancels cricket practice and hurts both a bat seller and a ball seller. Two products can still share one shock.
concepts.rule: Spreading money across many firms and industries can cut the harm from one weak part. It cannot make all loss go away, since many parts can fall together.

claims.text: A mix of holdings can spread the risk from one firm.
A broad mix can cut some risk from one firm. It cannot promise you will not lose if the whole market drops.
Four or five shares are not a real spread. One investor guide asks for at least a dozen, across many industries.
A fund that holds just one industry does not give a full spread on its own.
Each extra holding can add fees, and fees lower your returns.

items.stem: One of your equal holdings went to zero, and your whole mix fell about 5%. About how many holdings do you have?

options.text: About 20.
options.feedback: Each holding is one part of the whole. If one part is 5%, there are 100 ÷ 5 = 20 parts.

options.text: About 5.
options.feedback: Five is the percent that fell, not the count. One part worth 5% means 20 equal parts.

options.text: About 95, the share that was left.
options.feedback: The 95% left is a percent, not a count. One holding worth 5% means 20 holdings in all.

items.stem: At the college canteen, Rohan's stall sells cold drinks, tea and snacks. Which trouble does his mix of goods soften: a cold week, or a strike that shuts the canteen?

options.text: The cold week, since tea and snacks still sell.
options.feedback: Right. A mix helps when one line slumps. A shutdown stops every line at once, so the mix cannot help there.

options.text: The strike, since he has three kinds of goods.
options.feedback: A shutdown stops all sales together. Having three kinds of goods only helps when one of them slumps alone.

options.text: Both, as a mix guards against any kind of loss.
options.feedback: A mix softens one weak line, not a shock that hits everything at once, like the whole canteen closing.

items.stem: Splitting ₹8,000 as ₹7,000 in one firm and ₹1,000 in another barely helps, because ___.

options.text: the two firm names make the money well spread
options.feedback: Names alone do not make a spread. Most of this money still depends on one firm.

options.text: two firms mean a market fall cannot hurt the money
options.feedback: A mix can still fall with the market. Here most of the money also rests on one firm.

items.stem: Fifteen shares, all in steel firms, make a weak spread, because ___.

options.text: firms in one industry rise and fall together
options.feedback: Right. One industry's slump hits every firm in it, so many names in one industry still share one fate.

options.text: fifteen is far too many shares for one person to hold
options.feedback: A dozen or more firms is a good count. The trouble is that all fifteen sit in one industry.

options.text: the steel firms have separate names, so their risks cannot overlap
options.feedback: Different names in one industry can share risks. A broader mix spreads firm risk better.

items.stem: Aman says his pharma fund is a full spread on its own, since it holds 40 firms. What is not quite right?

options.text: All 40 are in one industry, so they tend to move together.

options.text: Forty is too few; a spread needs hundreds of firms.
options.feedback: The count is not his trouble. A spread needs firms in different industries, and all of his are pharma.

options.text: Nothing; any fund with 40 firms is fully spread.
options.feedback: Forty firms in one industry still share the same risk, so the fund is not a full spread.

options.text: Twelve clubs keep total sales steady.
options.feedback: Many stalls help only when trouble hits one of them. A cancelled fest hits every stall.

options.text: The food stalls lose sales, the rest do fine.
options.feedback: The warning cancels everything, so every kind of stall loses its buyers at once.

concepts.title: What a stock is
concepts.hook: One share makes a student a tiny owner of a company, with a vote at its general meeting. It does not promise any dividend.
concepts.rule: A share is a small ownership piece of a company. Owners can vote at the general meeting. A dividend may be paid, but it is never promised.

claims.text: A share gives part ownership of a company.
A firm may pay a share of its gains. The payout is not sure. Owners can also benefit if the company grows.
The more shares you hold, the bigger the piece of the company you own.
Owners of shares can vote on big decisions at the firm's general meeting.

concepts.title: Emergency fund
concepts.hook: A sudden repair bill is easier to meet when money is already set aside and easy to reach.
concepts.rule: An emergency fund is money kept for a sudden need. Aim for at least three months of living costs, kept in a separate, easy-to-reach savings account. Starting small still helps.

claims.text: An emergency fund is cash kept for a sudden need.
The reserve is useful when it can be reached without waiting for a sale.
The RBI guide suggests at least three months of living costs, or six months or more if your job is less secure or you run a business.
The guide says to keep it in a savings account that is easy to reach and separate from other savings.
If you cannot fund it all now, the guide says to start small and save a little from each pay.

options.text: No; it was known ahead, so it is a planning gap.

options.text: Emergency fund cost

steps.title: Money set aside only for surprises

hook.stem: Which of these is an emergency fund meant to pay for?

options.text: A sudden hospital bill.
options.feedback: Right. The fund is for costs nobody planned, like a sudden illness.

options.text: A trip planned for months.
options.feedback: A planned trip is a known cost. The fund is kept for surprises.

options.text: This month's phone recharge.
options.feedback: A recharge comes every month, so it belongs in your budget, not the fund.

steps.title: Keep it easy to reach, and apart

hook.stem: Where is an emergency fund best kept?

options.text: In shares, for the most growth.

options.text: Lent to a friend.

concepts.title: EMI and loan cost
concepts.hook: A smaller monthly EMI can still lead to more total interest when a loan runs longer.
concepts.rule: An EMI pays interest and some principal. Interest is based on what is still owed, and a longer term means a smaller EMI but more interest in total.

claims.text: An EMI can pay loan interest and part of the loan sum. On a fixed-rate loan the EMI stays the same each month.
As a loan shrinks, later interest uses the sum still due.
A longer loan term makes each EMI smaller but means paying more interest in total.
In the RBI example, a ₹10 lakh loan at 15% over 120 months has an EMI of ₹16,133.50, and ₹12,500 of the first EMI is interest.

items.stem: Stretching a loan over more months raises its total cost, because ___.

options.text: interest keeps running for longer
options.feedback: Right. Each EMI is smaller, but interest is charged for more months, so the total paid goes up.

options.text: the rate goes up each extra month
options.feedback: The rate can stay the same. The total rises because interest is charged for more months.

options.text: smaller EMIs carry a late fee
options.feedback: Smaller EMIs are not late payments. The extra cost is interest charged over more months.

options.text: No; the fee is a cost of borrowing, about 5% of the price.

options.text: Yes; with no interest, it costs no more.
options.feedback: Interest is one cost of a loan, not the only one. The ₹1,500 fee is paid on top.

options.text: Yes, as long as each EMI is the same size.
options.feedback: Equal EMIs say nothing about cost. The ₹1,500 fee still makes the phone dearer.

options.feedback: Yes. The EMI is interest plus principal, so ₹9,000 minus ₹6,500 leaves ₹2,500 of interest.
That adds the two. The principal part sits inside the EMI, so subtract it instead.
That is the whole EMI. Most of it cuts the principal, leaving ₹2,500 as interest.

options.text: About ₹9.4 lakh.

options.text: About ₹1.5 lakh.
options.feedback: That is 15% for one year only. Interest is paid every month for ten years.

options.text: About ₹19.4 lakh.
options.feedback: That is everything paid back. The ₹10 lakh borrowed is not interest.

options.text: The rate matters, not the term.
options.feedback: At the same rate, a longer term charges interest for more months, so the term matters too.

options.text: It stays the same each month.

options.text: The 2-year loan.
options.feedback: Its EMIs are bigger, but interest stops sooner, so its total interest is lower.

options.text: They cost the same.

options.text: Any term, since the rate is the same.
options.feedback: The rate is the same, but the time differs, so the totals differ.

steps.takeaway: A longer loan lowers each EMI but raises the total interest.

concepts.title: Index funds and stock picking
concepts.hook: An index fund holds a whole basket of companies. One chosen stock rides on a single company.
concepts.rule: An index fund copies an index's firms in the same mix, with low fees. It rises and falls with that index, a little behind after costs.

claims.text: An index fund holds securities to follow a named index and charges an expense ratio.
Over ten years, most active large-cap funds in India did worse than their index. The share varies by year and fund group.
An index fund holds all or most of the shares in its index, in the same proportions, instead of relying on a manager to pick.
Index funds follow a passive plan with little trading, so their expense ratios are lower than active funds.
Tracking error is the small gap between an index fund and its index, caused by expenses and running costs.

options.text: An index fund.

options.text: An active fund, run by a manager.

options.text: A fixed deposit.
options.feedback: A deposit earns a bank rate and holds no list of firms at all.

options.text: The index list and its mix.
options.feedback: Yes. The fund holds what the index holds, in the same proportions, with no one choosing.

options.text: The manager's own research.
options.feedback: That is how an active fund works. An index fund just follows its list.

options.text: Whichever firms rose most last month.
options.feedback: Recent winners do not decide it. The fund copies its index, whatever the firms did lately.

steps.title: An index fund copies a list

hook.stem: The Nifty 50 is a list of 50 Indian companies. What does a Nifty 50 index fund hold?

options.text: The same 50 firms, in the same mix.
options.feedback: Right. It holds the shares on the list in the same proportions as the index.

options.text: A manager's ten favourite picks.
options.feedback: No one picks favourites. The fund simply copies the list.

options.text: Only the biggest company.
options.feedback: It holds all or most of the firms on the list, not just one.

steps.teach: An index is a list of companies, like the Nifty 50. An index fund holds the shares on that list, in the same mix, so no one picks.

example.ask: Tap what decides the fund's holdings.
parts: Mahi's fund follows a big index,
so it holds the firms on that list in the same mix,
and no one picks favourites.
example.spot: so it holds the firms on that list in the same mix,
example.feedback: The index list sets what the fund holds and how much of each.

guided.stem: A company joins the index. What does the index fund do?
guided.hint: The fund follows the list.

options.text: Adds that company too.
options.feedback: Yes. The fund copies the index, so a new member joins the fund.

options.text: Ignores it.
options.feedback: Ignoring changes would stop the fund matching the index.

options.text: Waits for its manager to judge the company.
options.feedback: No one picks in an index fund, so the fund adds the new member. An active fund is the kind that pays a manager to pick.

steps.takeaway: An index fund holds the index's firms in the index's mix.

steps.title: No picking means lower costs

hook.stem: Why are index funds usually cheaper to run than active funds?

options.text: No one is paid to pick shares.
options.feedback: Right. Following a list takes little research or trading, so the fee is lower.

options.text: Fees are banned for them.
options.feedback: Index funds do charge a fee. It is just lower, since there is little to manage.

options.text: They hold fewer firms.
options.feedback: Many hold more firms than active funds. The saving comes from not picking.

steps.teach: Index funds follow a list and trade little, so their yearly fee, the expense ratio, is usually lower. Over ten years, most active large-cap funds trailed their index.

example.ask: Tap why the fee is lower.
parts: Kunal's index fund rarely trades,
because it only follows its list,
so it charges a lower fee.
example.spot: because it only follows its list,
example.feedback: With no stock picking and little trading, the fund costs less to run.

guided.stem: Fund X charges 1% a year and Fund Y charges 0.2%. Both follow the same index. Which keeps more of the index's return?
guided.hint: The fee comes out of the return.

options.text: Fund Y.
options.feedback: Yes. Its lower fee takes less out. Over ten years, most active large-cap funds in India did worse than their index.

options.text: Fund X, since a higher fee means better care.
options.feedback: Both just follow the same list, so a higher fee buys nothing extra. X keeps less.

options.text: Fund X, for better picks.
options.feedback: Both just follow the same index. No one picks, so the extra fee only takes more out.

steps.takeaway: No stock picking keeps index fund fees low.

steps.title: It follows the index, ups and downs, a little behind

options.text: Far more than 10%.
options.feedback: An index fund aims to match its index, not beat it.

concepts.title: UPI scams and social engineering
concepts.hook: A fake prize message may ask for a UPI PIN to make a payment look like a receipt.
concepts.rule: A scam story can steer a person to approve a payment. A UPI PIN approves payments; receiving never needs it. No one else needs your PIN or OTP. If tricked, tell your bank and call 1930.

claims.text: NPCI warns that a QR scan and UPI PIN can be used to make a payment, not collect a prize.

Since 1 October 2025, people can no longer send each other UPI collect requests; merchants still can, for genuine business use. Scam messages also use links or QR codes that promise rewards for your PIN.
RBI says getting money never needs a QR scan or a PIN, so take care if asked for either.
RBI says never share your UPI PIN or OTP with anyone, not even bank staff, and not to download unknown apps on your phone.
RBI says to tell your bank at once about a debit you did not make, and block debits, including UPI. Money taken by fraud can be reported on the 1930 helpline or cybercrime.gov.in.

items.stem: Match each UPI moment to what it means for your money.

options.text: Entering your UPI PIN
options.feedback: Your PIN is your approval, so money leaves your account.

options.text: Rupees leave you
options.feedback: Money only leaves when you approve a payment with your PIN.

options.text: A friend paying you back
options.feedback: When a friend sends you money, you do nothing but receive it.

options.text: Nothing to type
options.feedback: Getting money needs no PIN and no scan from you.

options.text: Scanning a stranger's QR code
options.feedback: A QR scan sets up a payment from you to whoever made the code.

options.text: Starts a payment out
options.feedback: This is what a scan does: it opens a payment from your account.

items.stem: You buy groceries and scan the shop's UPI QR code to pay the bill. Is entering your PIN right here?

options.text: Yes; you mean to pay, so the PIN approves your own payment.
options.feedback: Right. The PIN is meant for paying. The trick is only when someone says it will bring money in.

options.text: No; a PIN should not be typed on a QR payment.
options.feedback: You do need your PIN to pay. Just never enter it to receive money or share it.

options.text: Only if the shop sends you money first.
options.feedback: Paying a shop needs no money from them. Your PIN simply approves your payment.

items.stem: Three links each ask for your UPI PIN to claim ₹1,500 'cashback'. If you enter your PIN on all three, about how much leaves you?

options.text: About ₹4,500.
options.feedback: Each PIN entry approves a ₹1,500 payment. Three times ₹1,500 is ₹4,500 out of your account.

options.text: About ₹1,500 comes in.
options.feedback: A PIN never brings money in. Each entry sends ₹1,500 out.

options.text: Nothing, since cashback is free.
options.feedback: The cashback label is the bait. Each PIN entry is a real payment of ₹1,500.

items.stem: A caller who gets your OTP can move your money, because the OTP ___.

options.text: approves payments as if it were you
options.feedback: Yes. The OTP is a key for approving a payment, so whoever has it can act as you.

options.text: lets bank staff safely approve a payment
options.feedback: Bank staff do not need your OTP. It can approve a payment or login, so it must stay secret.

options.text: stops working after one second
options.feedback: It lasts long enough to be used, which is why a scammer asks for it at once.

items.stem: Riya saw a UPI debit she never made, so she called her bank at once and blocked UPI. The scammer tried two more debits, but both were blocked. What made the difference?

options.text: Telling the bank fast, before more could leave.
options.feedback: Right. Blocking UPI quickly shut the door, so the later debits could not go through.

options.text: Her bank returns any stolen money by itself, at once.
options.feedback: Banks cannot promise to return money. What stopped the later debits was how fast she blocked UPI.

options.text: She could approve those requests first and cancel them later.
options.feedback: Approval can make a payment. Her quick report and UPI block stopped the later debits.

items.stem: A scam text reached you, but you did not tap its link and your money is safe. Is there anything to report?

options.text: Yes; report it on Chakshu.
options.feedback: Right. Chakshu takes reports of suspected fraud calls and texts, which can help stop the scammer.

options.text: No; reports are just for money taken.
options.feedback: Suspected fraud messages can be reported too, through Chakshu on Sanchar Saathi.

options.text: Reply to the text to warn the sender off.
options.feedback: Replying only keeps you in touch with the scammer. Report the text on Chakshu instead.

misconceptions.name: PIN to receive
misconceptions.correction: To get money, a person need not key in a UPI PIN.

misconceptions.name: Official tone proves safety
misconceptions.correction: A neat bank-like note can still tell a false story.

misconceptions.name: Bank staff may know your PIN
misconceptions.correction: No one, not even bank staff, needs your PIN or OTP.

misconceptions.name: Approve now, cancel later
misconceptions.correction: Entering your PIN on any request, link or QR code is the payment itself.

misconceptions.name: Scanning a QR can get you money
misconceptions.correction: A QR scan and UPI PIN can make a payment; getting money needs neither.

steps.title: Your PIN sends money; it never receives it

hook.stem: A buyer on a resale site says, 'Scan my QR code and enter your PIN to get paid.' What will happen?

options.text: Money will leave your account.
options.feedback: Right. Getting money never needs a scan or a PIN, so this sends money out.

options.text: The payment will come in.
options.feedback: Receiving needs no PIN at all. Entering it approves a payment from you.

options.text: It just checks your account.
options.feedback: Entering your PIN on this request approves a payment, not a simple check.

steps.teach: Getting money on UPI needs no PIN and no QR scan, because your PIN only approves money going out. So a request for it to get paid is a trick.

example.ask: Tap the red flag.
parts: Ankit sells his old cycle online,
and the buyer asks him to enter his UPI PIN
to receive the ₹3,000.
example.spot: and the buyer asks him to enter his UPI PIN
example.feedback: Receiving money never needs a PIN, so this request is a trick to make him pay.

guided.stem: You are getting a ₹500 refund. What do you need to type in?
guided.hint: Think about which way the rupees travel.

options.text: Nothing, since money coming in needs no PIN.
options.feedback: Yes. Money coming to you needs no PIN and no scan.

options.text: Your UPI PIN.
options.feedback: A PIN approves money going out. A refund coming in needs none.

options.text: Your OTP.
options.feedback: No OTP is needed to receive money. Never share one with anyone.

steps.takeaway: Your PIN approves payments. Receiving money never needs it.

steps.title: Never share your PIN, OTP or screen

hook.stem: A caller says he is from your bank and needs your UPI PIN to update your KYC. What is the right reply?

options.text: Refuse, since no one needs your PIN.
options.feedback: Right. No real bank worker ever needs your PIN, however genuine the caller sounds.

options.text: Share it, since he knows your name.
options.feedback: Scammers often know names. Knowing yours does not make him safe.

options.text: Give it, but change the PIN later.
options.feedback: By then the money can be gone. A PIN is never shared at all.

steps.teach: Your UPI PIN or OTP approves a payment, so whoever has it can move your money. Never share either, even with a caller claiming to be bank staff.

right.title: Unsafe
lines: Read out a PIN or OTP
Install an app a caller names

example.ask: Tap the mistake.
parts: Manav finds a 'bank helpline' through a web search,
the man who answers asks for his OTP,
and Manav reads it out to him.
example.spot: and Manav reads it out to him.
example.feedback: Sharing an OTP hands over the key to his account, so it is never shared, even with bank staff.

guided.stem: A caller asks you to install a screen-sharing app to 'fix' your refund. What is the safe move?
guided.hint: Think about what he could watch on your phone.

options.text: Refuse and hang up.
options.feedback: Right. An app like that lets a stranger see or steer your phone, so never install one for a caller.

options.text: Install it, but do not type your PIN.
options.feedback: He could still watch codes and messages arrive. Do not install apps a caller asks for.

options.text: Install it if he calls from the bank's number.
options.feedback: A caller's number can be faked, and real bank staff never ask you to install apps.

steps.takeaway: Your PIN, OTP and screen are for you alone, never for callers.

steps.title: If you are tricked, act fast and report it

hook.stem: Money just left your account through a trick. What do you do first?

options.text: Tell your bank at once and block UPI.
options.feedback: Right. Acting fast can stop more money leaving your account.

options.text: Wait a day to see if it comes back.
options.feedback: Waiting gives the scammer time. Tell your bank straight away.

options.text: Keep quiet, since it was your mistake.
options.feedback: Being tricked is common and not shameful. Acting fast is what helps.

steps.teach: If tricked, act fast, since speed can stop more money leaving. Tell your bank and block UPI, then call 1930 or use cybercrime.gov.in.

example.ask: Tap the first thing she does.
parts: Rhea sees a debit SMS she did not expect,
so she calls her bank and blocks UPI at once,
then reports it on 1930.
example.spot: so she calls her bank and blocks UPI at once,
example.feedback: Telling the bank fast and blocking UPI can stop more money leaving, before she reports it.

guided.stem: Your friend was tricked last month and feels too ashamed to report it. What helps most?
guided.hint: Think about who the real wrongdoer is.

options.text: Report it anyway; scammers do this for a living.
options.feedback: Right. Being fooled by a skilled scammer is common, and reporting can help stop them.

options.text: Report it just if a big sum was taken.
options.feedback: Any fraud is worth reporting, since reports help stop scammers. They do this for a living, so there is no shame in it.

options.text: Delete the messages and forget it.
options.feedback: The messages are proof. Keep them and report the fraud.

steps.takeaway: Act fast: bank, then 1930. Report scam calls and texts on Chakshu.
